guides.title: Macronutrients, Micronutrients & How the Body Uses Them
guides.summary: First-principles nutrition science: the chemistry of carbohydrate, fat and protein, the Atwater energy factors, digestion and metabolic fate, vitamin and mineral functions with real requirement figures, deficiency syndromes, and how to compute your own energy and protein needs.

sections.heading: Definitions and the energy equation
sections.body:
A NUTRIENT is a chemical an organism must obtain from the environment because it cannot synthesise enough itself. Nutrients split by required quantity. MACRONUTRIENTS are needed in grams per day and supply energy and structure: carbohydrate, fat (lipid), protein — plus water. MICRONUTRIENTS are needed in milligrams (mg = 10⁻³ g) or micrograms (µg = 10⁻⁶ g): 13 vitamins and about 15 essential minerals. Micronutrients yield NO energy; they act as enzyme cofactors, hormones, antioxidants or structural ions. ESSENTIAL means the body cannot synthesise it at all (vitamin C, the amino acid lysine, the fatty acid linoleic acid). CONDITIONALLY ESSENTIAL means synthesis exists but fails under stress, growth or illness (glutamine, arginine).
Energy is measured in kilocalories (kcal) or kilojoules (kJ): 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ. One kcal raises 1 kg of water by 1 °C. The capital-C "Calorie" on a food label IS the kilocalorie.
Metabolisable energy is estimated by the ATWATER GENERAL FACTORS:
  E = 4·C + 4·P + 9·F + 7·A + 2·Fb
where E = kcal, C = grams digestible carbohydrate, P = grams protein, F = grams fat, A = grams ethanol, Fb = grams fermentable fibre. Each coefficient is kcal per gram: the gross heat of combustion minus faecal and urinary losses. Fat carries 9 kcal/g because its carbons are highly reduced (few oxygens) so oxidising them releases more energy; carbohydrate carbons are already partly oxidised. Protein loses ~1.25 kcal/g to urea excreted in urine, which is why its factor is 4 and not 5.3.

sections.heading: Carbohydrate: structure, digestion, glycaemic behaviour
sections.body:
Carbohydrates are (CH₂O)ₙ compounds. Classes:
• MONOSACCHARIDES — single sugar units: glucose, fructose, galactose (all C₆H₁₂O₆, differing in geometry).
• DISACCHARIDES — two units: sucrose (glucose+fructose), lactose (glucose+galactose), maltose (glucose+glucose).
• OLIGOSACCHARIDES — 3–10 units: raffinose, stachyose in beans (humans lack α-galactosidase, so gut bacteria ferment them → gas).
• POLYSACCHARIDES — starch (amylose, a straight α-1,4 chain; amylopectin, branched α-1,4/α-1,6) and fibre (cellulose is β-1,4 glucose — human amylase cannot cleave β bonds, so it passes undigested).
DIGESTION: salivary and pancreatic α-amylase cut starch to maltose and dextrins; brush-border enzymes (maltase, sucrase, lactase) finish the job; monosaccharides cross the intestinal wall (glucose and galactose by the sodium-coupled SGLT1 transporter, fructose by GLUT5) into portal blood.
Blood glucose is held near 4.0–5.5 mmol/L (72–99 mg/dL) fasting. Insulin from pancreatic β-cells drives glucose into muscle and fat; glucagon and adrenaline release it from liver glycogen. The liver stores about 100 g of glycogen (≈400 kcal), muscle about 400 g (usable only locally). Once glycogen is full, surplus carbohydrate is converted to fat (de novo lipogenesis), an inefficient route costing ~25% of the energy.
There is NO dietary requirement for carbohydrate in the strict sense — the brain's ~120 g/day glucose demand can be met by gluconeogenesis from amino acids and glycerol plus ketone bodies — but most healthy diets supply 45–65% of energy as carbohydrate. Fibre intake of 25–38 g/day feeds colonic bacteria that produce short-chain fatty acids (butyrate, propionate, acetate) which nourish the colon lining.

sections.heading: Fat: fatty acids, essentiality and transport
sections.body:
Dietary fat is ~95% TRIGLYCERIDE: a glycerol backbone esterified to three fatty acids. A fatty acid is a hydrocarbon chain with a carboxyl (–COOH) end. Notation: 18:2 n-6 means 18 carbons, 2 double bonds, first double bond 6 carbons from the methyl (omega, n) end.
• SATURATED (no double bonds; e.g. palmitic 16:0, stearic 18:0) — solid at room temperature, chemically stable, high smoke point.
• MONOUNSATURATED (one; oleic 18:1 n-9, the main fat of olive oil).
• POLYUNSATURATED (two or more; linoleic 18:2 n-6 and alpha-linolenic 18:3 n-3). These two are the only strictly ESSENTIAL fatty acids — humans lack the desaturase enzymes to insert a double bond beyond carbon 9. Deficiency (scaly dermatitis, poor wound healing) is prevented by roughly 2–4% of energy as linoleic and 0.5–1% as alpha-linolenic — a tablespoon of most seed oils or a handful of nuts daily.
• TRANS fats from partial hydrogenation raise LDL and lower HDL cholesterol; industrial trans fat is now banned or restricted in most jurisdictions.
DIGESTION: bile salts from the gallbladder emulsify fat into micelles (increasing surface area for enzymes roughly 1000-fold); pancreatic lipase splits triglyceride into 2-monoglyceride + 2 free fatty acids; these diffuse into enterocytes, are reassembled into triglyceride and packaged into CHYLOMICRONS which enter the LYMPH (not the portal vein) and reach blood via the thoracic duct — which is why fat absorption bypasses first-pass liver metabolism.
Fat also carries the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K; a near-zero-fat diet impairs their absorption. Body fat stores are effectively unlimited: 1 kg of adipose tissue holds about 7,700 kcal of usable energy (it is ~87% lipid, not 100%).

sections.heading: Protein: amino acids, quality and turnover
sections.body:
Proteins are polymers of 20 standard AMINO ACIDS, each with an amino group (–NH₂), a carboxyl group (–COOH) and a distinguishing side chain (R group), joined by peptide bonds. Nine are ESSENTIAL for adults: histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine (mnemonic: "PVT TIM HaLL").
PROTEIN QUALITY is judged by whether the pattern of essential amino acids matches human need. The LIMITING AMINO ACID is the essential one in shortest supply relative to requirement; it caps how much of the rest can be used. Cereals (wheat, rice, maize) are limiting in LYSINE; legumes (beans, lentils, peas) are limiting in METHIONINE. Combining them — beans and rice, hummus and pita, dal and chapati — gives a complete pattern. The old belief that complementary proteins must be eaten in the same meal is obsolete: the body maintains a free amino-acid pool for many hours, so complementation across a day is sufficient.
Scoring systems: PDCAAS (Protein Digestibility-Corrected Amino Acid Score, 0–1.00; egg, milk, soy ≈ 1.00; wheat ≈ 0.42) and the newer DIAAS. Digestibility matters — cooking legumes destroys trypsin inhibitors and raises usable protein substantially.
REQUIREMENT: the adult RDA is 0.80 g protein per kg body mass per day, which covers 97.5% of the population. Endurance athletes need ~1.2–1.6 g/kg; strength athletes and older adults preserving muscle do better at 1.6–2.0 g/kg. Protein cannot be stored as protein: excess is deaminated, the nitrogen excreted as urea (which requires water — high protein intake raises fluid needs), and the carbon skeleton burned or stored as fat. Body protein turns over at roughly 250–300 g/day, most of it recycled.

sections.heading: The 13 vitamins: function, sources, deficiency
sections.body:
FAT-SOLUBLE (stored in liver and adipose; overdose is possible):
• A (retinol; RDA ≈ 900 µg RAE men / 700 women) — rhodopsin for night vision, epithelial integrity, immunity. Liver, egg yolk, dairy; plant β-carotene in carrots, sweet potato, dark greens. Deficiency: night blindness → xerophthalmia → blindness. Excess (>3,000 µg/d preformed) is teratogenic; polar-bear or seal liver has caused acute toxicity.
• D (cholecalciferol; 15–20 µg = 600–800 IU/d) — calcium absorption, bone mineralisation, immune modulation. Synthesised in skin from 7-dehydrocholesterol under UVB. Deficiency: rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults.
• E (α-tocopherol; 15 mg/d) — lipid-membrane antioxidant. Vegetable oils, nuts, seeds.
• K (phylloquinone; ~90–120 µg/d) — γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X. Leafy greens; also made by colonic bacteria. Newborns get an injection because placental transfer is poor.
WATER-SOLUBLE (excess mostly excreted; must be resupplied often):
• B1 thiamin (1.1–1.2 mg) — pyruvate dehydrogenase cofactor. Deficiency: beriberi (wet = heart failure, dry = neuropathy); classically from polished white rice.
• B2 riboflavin (1.1–1.3 mg), B3 niacin (14–16 mg NE; deficiency = pellagra: dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia, death — historic in maize-dependent populations because maize niacin is bound unless nixtamalised with alkali), B5 pantothenate (5 mg), B6 pyridoxine (1.3 mg, amino-acid metabolism), B7 biotin (30 µg), B9 folate (400 µg DFE; 600 µg in pregnancy — prevents neural-tube defects), B12 cobalamin (2.4 µg; found ONLY in animal foods and fortified products — vegans MUST supplement; deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia and irreversible nerve damage).
• C ascorbate (75–90 mg) — collagen hydroxylation, iron absorption, antioxidant. Deficiency: scurvy (bleeding gums, reopening of old wounds) after roughly 4–12 weeks of near-zero intake; as little as 10 mg/day prevents it. Human beings, guinea pigs and some bats lack the gulonolactone oxidase enzyme other mammals use to make their own.

sections.heading: Essential minerals and electrolytes
sections.body:
MAJOR MINERALS (needed >100 mg/day):
• Calcium 1,000–1,200 mg — bone (99% of body calcium), muscle contraction, clotting. Dairy, canned fish with bones, calcium-set tofu, greens. Absorption ~30% and requires vitamin D.
• Phosphorus 700 mg — ATP, DNA, bone. Ubiquitous.
• Magnesium 310–420 mg — cofactor for >300 enzymes including all ATP-using ones. Nuts, seeds, legumes, whole grains, greens.
• Sodium ~1,500 mg adequate, upper limit ~2,300 mg (≈5.8 g salt) — extracellular fluid volume, nerve impulses. Potassium 2,600–3,400 mg — intracellular cation, blood-pressure lowering. Chloride — stomach acid, HCl.
TRACE MINERALS (<100 mg/day): iron 8 mg men / 18 mg premenopausal women (haemoglobin oxygen transport; heme iron from meat absorbs at 15–35%, non-heme from plants at 2–20% and is boosted several-fold by vitamin C eaten in the same meal and inhibited by tea tannins and phytate); zinc 8–11 mg (>300 enzymes, immunity, wound healing); iodine 150 µg (thyroid hormones T3/T4 — deficiency causes goitre and, in pregnancy, permanent cognitive impairment; iodised salt is the cheapest public-health intervention in history); selenium 55 µg (glutathione peroxidase); copper, manganese, molybdenum, chromium, fluoride in µg–mg amounts.
Electrolyte balance is life-critical: severe sweating loses roughly 1 g sodium per litre of sweat. Drinking large volumes of plain water while sweating heavily for hours can cause EXERCISE-ASSOCIATED HYPONATRAEMIA (blood sodium <135 mmol/L) — confusion, seizures, death. Oral rehydration solution (WHO formula: 2.6 g NaCl + 13.5 g glucose + 1.5 g KCl + 2.9 g trisodium citrate per litre; improvised: 6 level teaspoons sugar + ½ teaspoon salt in 1 L clean water) exploits sodium-glucose co-transport, which keeps working even in cholera-damaged gut.

sections.heading: Worked example: computing one person's needs
sections.body:
Subject: 34-year-old man, 78 kg, 178 cm, moderately active.
STEP 1 — Basal Metabolic Rate by the Mifflin–St Jeor equation:
  BMR (kcal/day) = 10·W + 6.25·H − 5·A + 5 (men) or −161 (women)
  W = mass in kg, H = height in cm, A = age in years.
  BMR = 10(78) + 6.25(178) − 5(34) + 5 = 780 + 1112.5 − 170 + 5 = 1,727 kcal/day.
STEP 2 — Total Daily Energy Expenditure: TDEE = BMR × PAL, where PAL (Physical Activity Level) is 1.2 sedentary, 1.4 light, 1.55 moderate, 1.75 heavy, 2.0+ very heavy manual labour.
  TDEE = 1,727 × 1.55 ≈ 2,677 kcal/day.
STEP 3 — Protein: 78 kg × 0.8 = 62 g/day minimum; at 1.6 g/kg for training, 125 g/day = 500 kcal.
STEP 4 — Fat: set at 25–35% of energy. At 30%: 0.30 × 2,677 = 803 kcal ÷ 9 = 89 g/day. Ensure at least ~17 g linoleic acid and 1.6 g alpha-linolenic.
STEP 5 — Carbohydrate fills the remainder: 2,677 − 500 − 803 = 1,374 kcal ÷ 4 = 344 g/day, of which ≥30 g should be fibre.
CHECK against real food: 500 g cooked rice (~650 kcal, 13 g protein), 200 g chicken breast (~330 kcal, 62 g protein), 300 g mixed vegetables (~120 kcal), 60 g peanuts (~350 kcal, 15 g protein), 500 mL milk (~320 kcal, 17 g protein), 2 tbsp oil (~240 kcal), 2 slices bread (~160 kcal, 6 g protein) ≈ 2,170 kcal and 113 g protein — the gap of ~500 kcal is closed with fruit, extra grain or oil.
ENERGY BALANCE: an accumulated deficit of about 7,700 kcal corresponds to roughly 1 kg of body fat, though real weight change is slower than this arithmetic predicts because BMR falls as mass falls.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and safety notes
sections.body:
• Confusing calories with kilocalories by a factor of 1,000 when reading scientific versus consumer sources.
• Treating the Atwater factors as exact. They are averages; whole almonds, for example, deliver about 20% less energy than the label implies because intact cell walls resist digestion. Cooking and grinding raise available energy from the same food.
• Assuming "a calorie deficit" is the only variable. Protein adequacy, micronutrient adequacy and fibre determine whether weight loss costs you muscle, bone and immunity.
• Megadosing fat-soluble vitamins. Vitamin A above ~3,000 µg/day preformed retinol and vitamin D above ~100 µg (4,000 IU)/day long-term risk toxicity: hypercalcaemia, liver damage, birth defects. Water-soluble vitamins are safer but not harmless — B6 above ~100 mg/day for months causes sensory neuropathy; niacin above ~35 mg causes flushing and, at gram doses, liver injury.
• Iron supplementation without a diagnosed deficiency. Iron overload damages liver, heart and pancreas, and iron tablets are a leading cause of fatal poisoning in small children — store them locked away.
• Ignoring vitamin B12 on a plant-only diet. Damage from B12 deficiency can be permanent even after correction; the fix (a cheap 25–100 µg daily or 1,000 µg weekly tablet, or fortified foods) is trivial.
• Prolonged refeeding after starvation. Reintroducing carbohydrate to a severely malnourished person triggers REFEEDING SYNDROME: insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, and the resulting plasma collapse can kill within days. Refeeding must be slow (start ~10 kcal/kg/day) and supervised, with thiamin given first.
This guide is educational. Nutrition interacts with medication, pregnancy, kidney and liver disease. Seek qualified medical or dietetic care for diagnosis and treatment; do not self-treat suspected deficiency states that are causing symptoms.

sections.heading: Cellular Respiration: How Macronutrients Actually Become ATP
sections.body:
Digestion and absorption only get fuel to the doorstep of the cell; the actual "use" promised in this guide's title happens in the cytoplasm and mitochondria, and it is worth tracing all the way through because the numbers explain why fat is such a dense fuel and why the brain is so picky about glucose.

Glucose's first stop is glycolysis, a ten-enzyme sequence in the cytosol that splits one 6-carbon glucose into two 3-carbon pyruvate molecules. It costs 2 ATP to prime the molecule (hexokinase and phosphofructokinase both consume ATP) and repays 4 ATP plus 2 NADH downstream, for a net yield of 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose — and it runs with or without oxygen, which is why anaerobic muscle can still make some ATP during an all-out sprint. If oxygen is available, pyruvate is ferried into the mitochondrial matrix and decarboxylated by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex into acetyl-CoA (releasing 1 CO2 and generating 1 NADH per pyruvate — 2 per glucose). Acetyl-CoA then enters the citric acid cycle, a closed loop of eight reactions that, per turn, releases 2 CO2 and generates 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP (readily swapped for ATP) — and because each glucose yields two acetyl-CoA, the cycle turns twice per glucose.

The real payoff comes at the electron transport chain, where NADH and FADH2 hand electrons down protein complexes embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane, pumping protons out to build an electrochemical gradient that ATP synthase spins like a turbine to phosphorylate ADP. Using modern accounting (roughly 2.5 ATP per NADH, 1.5 ATP per FADH2 — lower than the classic 3:2 textbook figures because some of the gradient leaks and some is spent shuttling NADH's electrons across the mitochondrial membrane), one glucose nets out to about 30–32 ATP total. Fat tells a different story: a 16-carbon palmitate molecule is chopped into 8 acetyl-CoA units by beta-oxidation, a cycle that itself throws off 1 FADH2 and 1 NADH per cut, and by the time all 8 acetyl-CoA units have gone through the citric acid cycle too, the grand total is around 106 net ATP per molecule — the molecular reason a gram of fat carries about 9 kcal against carbohydrate's 4: more reduced carbon-hydrogen bonds per gram means more electrons to hand to oxygen. Protein's amino acids are deaminated (the amino group stripped off as ammonia, ultimately excreted as urea via the liver's urea cycle) and their carbon skeletons feed into glycolysis or the citric acid cycle at various entry points — which is why protein is a serviceable but clumsy fuel: the body has to dispose of nitrogen it never needed to burn.

sections.heading: Fed and Fasted: How Hormones Decide Which Fuel Gets Burned
sections.body:
Which of the pathways above actually runs at full tilt at any given moment is not left to chance — it is switched by two pancreatic hormones acting in opposition, and the switch has hard numeric limits worth knowing.

Within minutes of a carbohydrate-containing meal, rising blood glucose triggers the pancreatic beta cells to secrete insulin, which opens GLUT4 glucose transporters in muscle and fat cells, activates glycogen synthase so the liver and muscles pack incoming glucose into glycogen, and suppresses fat breakdown so fat cells store rather than release fatty acids. Glycogen storage is not unlimited: the liver holds roughly 80–120 g (enough to buffer blood glucose for about 12–24 hours of fasting) and skeletal muscle holds a much larger 300–400 g, but muscle glycogen is landlocked — muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so it can only burn its own glycogen locally and can never export glucose back into the blood to feed the brain.

As hours pass without food, falling glucose flips the switch: the pancreatic alpha cells secrete glucagon, which breaks liver (not muscle) glycogen back down to glucose and turns on gluconeogenesis — synthesis of new glucose from lactate, glycerol and amino-acid carbon skeletons. Once liver glycogen runs low, typically after roughly a day of fasting, fat becomes the dominant fuel, and the liver starts converting acetyl-CoA it can't fully burn (because oxaloacetate, the citric acid cycle's entry gate, is busy feeding gluconeogenesis) into ketone bodies — acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetone — which the brain, unable to burn fatty acids directly, can use as a substitute fuel once levels rise high enough, typically after 2–4 days of fasting or on carbohydrate intake sustained below roughly 20–50 g/day.

You can watch this whole system's output without opening a cell, because the ratio of CO2 produced to O2 consumed — the respiratory quotient (RQ) — shifts with fuel choice: pure carbohydrate oxidation gives RQ = 1.0, pure fat oxidation gives RQ ≈ 0.7 (fat is oxygen-poor per carbon, so more inhaled O2 is needed per CO2 exhaled), and a mixed diet sits around 0.8–0.85 at rest. Metabolic carts used in exercise-physiology labs measure exactly this ratio through a mouthpiece to tell, non-invasively, which fuel tank a person is currently drawing down.

sections.heading: Equipment You'll Actually Need to Watch Your Own Metabolism at Work
sections.body: Everything below is sold over the counter with no prescription required, and together it turns the abstract chemistry above into numbers you can read off your own body.
ingredients: A digital kitchen scale accurate to 1 g (any basic model from a kitchen-supply or home-goods store) — needed to weigh food to a known carbohydrate content rather than guess.

An over-the-counter blood glucose meter with lancing device, lancets and test strips (sold without a prescription in the diabetes-testing aisle of any pharmacy) — the single most informative tool here.
Urine ketone test strips (same pharmacy aisle) or, for more precision, a blood ketone meter that uses a second type of test strip — used to detect the ketogenesis threshold described above.
A simple stopwatch or your phone's timer, to hold consistent intervals between readings.
A notebook or a free food-tracking phone app with a nutrition database, to log exact grams of carbohydrate, protein and fat eaten.
A bathroom scale and a cloth tape measure — optional, but useful context for tracking energy balance over weeks.

A rigid single-use sharps disposal container (a proper one from a pharmacy, or any hard-sided plastic bottle with a lid) — required for safe lancet disposal; never put used lancets loose in household trash.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Testing Your Own Glycemic Response and Fuel-Switching Threshold
sections.body: This two-part experiment lets you see the insulin/glucagon switch and the RQ shift described above acting on your own body, using nothing but a meter and a clock. It is self-education, not diagnosis — anyone with diagnosed diabetes, a history of hypoglycemia, or any condition affecting blood sugar should attempt this only with their doctor's guidance and a known safe glucose range.
steps: On a normal morning, fast for at least 8 hours (water only), then wash your hands and take a fasting blood glucose reading with the meter; write down the number and the exact time.

Weigh out a food containing exactly 50 g of available carbohydrate (about 65 g of dry white rice before cooking, or check a package label and do the arithmetic) and eat it within 5 minutes, alone, with no added fat or fiber-heavy sides that would slow absorption.
Take a fingerstick glucose reading at 15, 30, 45, 60, 90 and 120 minutes after the first bite, logging each value with its exact timestamp.

Plot the six points on graph paper or a spreadsheet; note the peak value, the time it occurred, and whether the 120-minute value has returned close to your fasting baseline — this curve is a rough personal glycemic-response profile.

On a separate day, repeat steps 1–3 with a different 50 g-carbohydrate food that differs in fiber or processing (a whole apple with skin instead of rice, say) and compare peak height and time-to-return between the two curves — this is the glycemic-index effect made visible on your own meter.

To observe the fasted-state switch, pick a day with no other obligations and extend an overnight fast to 16–18 hours, taking a glucose reading and a ketone reading every 3–4 hours; stop the fast and eat immediately if you feel dizzy, shaky, unwell, or your glucose reads below your doctor-confirmed normal range.

Note the clock time at which ketone strips first show a trace (light pink/purple) rather than reading negative — this marks, approximately, the point where liver glycogen has run low enough that ketogenesis has switched on, consistent with the 12–24 hour range described above.

Dispose of every used lancet and test strip in the sharps container, never loose in the trash, and keep all sessions logged in one place so you have a written personal record of both curves to refer back to.

guides.title: Food Preservation — Canning, Drying, Salting & Curing
guides.summary: The physics and microbiology of making food last: water activity, pH, thermal death curves, the acid/low-acid divide that governs botulism risk, plus step-by-step procedures with real temperatures, times, brine concentrations and salt ratios for canning, drying, salting, curing and smoking.

sections.heading: Why food spoils — the four hurdles
sections.body:
Food degrades by four independent routes: (1) MICROBIAL growth — bacteria, yeasts and moulds consuming the food and producing toxins; (2) ENZYMATIC action — the food's own enzymes (polyphenol oxidase browning a cut apple, lipases making fat rancid); (3) CHEMICAL oxidation — atmospheric O₂ attacking fats and pigments; (4) PHYSICAL damage — insects, rodents, freezer burn, crushing.
Preservation works by removing what microbes need. The HURDLE CONCEPT (Leistner) says several modest obstacles combined beat one extreme one. The main hurdles:
• WATER ACTIVITY (aw) — the ratio of the water vapour pressure above the food to that above pure water at the same temperature: aw = p/p₀, a dimensionless number 0 to 1.00. Pure water = 1.00. Most spoilage bacteria stop below aw 0.91; Staphylococcus aureus manages 0.86; most yeasts stop at 0.88, most moulds at 0.80; the extreme osmophilic moulds and yeasts stop near 0.61. Honey (aw ≈ 0.60), dried grain (0.60–0.65), hard salami (0.82–0.86) and jam (0.80) are preserved chiefly by low aw.
• pH — pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], the negative base-10 logarithm of hydrogen-ion concentration in mol/L. Below pH 4.6, Clostridium botulinum cannot grow or produce toxin. This single number governs all canning safety.
• TEMPERATURE — the "danger zone" 5–60 °C (41–140 °F) is where pathogens multiply fastest; below 5 °C growth slows greatly, below −18 °C it stops (but does not kill).
• OXYGEN and chemical inhibitors — vacuum/anaerobic packing stops moulds and aerobic bacteria; nitrite, smoke phenols, acids, spices and competitive fermentation microbes suppress others.
Note the trap: removing oxygen removes the aerobes but FAVOURS anaerobes such as C. botulinum. Never rely on one hurdle alone.

sections.heading: The botulism divide: acid vs low-acid foods
sections.body:
Clostridium botulinum is a spore-forming, strictly anaerobic soil bacterium found worldwide. Its vegetative cells die at ordinary cooking temperatures, but its SPORES survive boiling (100 °C) for hours. In a sealed jar of low-acid food at room temperature the spores germinate and produce botulinum neurotoxin — the most poisonous substance known, lethal in nanogram quantities, causing descending paralysis and respiratory failure. The toxin (though not the spore) is destroyed by boiling for 10 minutes.
THE RULE:
• HIGH-ACID FOODS, pH ≤ 4.6 — fruits, jams, pickles, properly fermented krauts, tomatoes WITH added acid. These may be safely processed in a BOILING-WATER BATH at 100 °C, because C. botulinum cannot grow at that acidity; only yeasts, moulds and lactobacilli need killing.
• LOW-ACID FOODS, pH > 4.6 — all vegetables (beans, corn, carrots, potatoes), all meats, poultry, fish, soups, and plain tomatoes (borderline, pH 4.2–4.9 depending on variety and ripeness). These require a PRESSURE CANNER reaching 116–121 °C (241–250 °F) at 10–15 psi gauge pressure. There is no home substitute. A boiling-water bath, an oven, a microwave, a dishwasher, an "open-kettle" hot-fill or an electric multicooker without a validated canning programme CANNOT make low-acid canned food safe.
Acidification: to can tomatoes safely add 1 tablespoon bottled lemon juice (standardised acidity — fresh lemons vary) or ¼ teaspoon citric acid per pint (0.5 L) jar; double for quarts. Pickling brines should be at least 5% acetic acid vinegar diluted no more than 1:1 with water, giving a finished pH below 4.6.
The thermal death of spores follows first-order kinetics: log₁₀(N₀/N) = t / D_T, where N₀ and N are initial and surviving spore counts, t is time in minutes, and D_T is the decimal reduction time (minutes at temperature T to kill 90% of spores). For C. botulinum spores D₁₂₁ ≈ 0.21 min. Commercial sterility of low-acid food demands a "12-D" process — 12 × 0.21 ≈ 2.52 minutes at 121 °C at the coldest point of the jar, which is why published processing times (which allow for heat penetration through the food) run 20–100 minutes.

sections.heading: Water-bath canning, step by step
sections.body:
Equipment: deep pot with rack and lid (water must cover jars by 25–50 mm), tested jars free of nicks, NEW flat lids each time (the sealing compound is single-use), screw bands, jar lifter, bubble tool, clean cloths.
1. INSPECT jars — run a fingertip round each rim; discard any with a chip, since it will not seal.
2. WASH jars in hot soapy water and rinse. If the processing time is under 10 minutes, sterilise jars by boiling 10 minutes (add 1 minute per 300 m above 300 m elevation); longer processes sterilise the contents in situ.
3. PREPARE the food to a tested recipe — do not reduce the acid, sugar or vinegar, and do not thicken with flour or extra fat, both of which slow heat penetration.
4. FILL hot jars with hot product, leaving the specified HEADSPACE: 6 mm (¼ in) for jams and jellies, 12 mm (½ in) for most fruits and pickles. Too little headspace and the contents boil out and foul the seal; too much and the air is not driven out.
5. DE-BUBBLE with a plastic tool round the inside, re-check headspace, WIPE the rim with a clean damp cloth (a smear of food or oil ruins the seal), place the lid, and screw the band "fingertip tight" — snug, not forced, so air can escape during processing.
6. PROCESS: lower jars onto the rack in simmering water, cover with 25–50 mm of water, bring to a full rolling boil, and START TIMING ONLY THEN. Typical: strawberry jam 10 min, peach halves in syrup 20–25 min (pints), dill cucumbers 10–15 min.
7. ALTITUDE CORRECTION — water boils cooler as you climb (about 1 °C per 285 m; 100 °C at sea level, 95 °C at 1,500 m, 90 °C at 3,000 m). Add 1 minute of boiling-water processing for each 300 m (1,000 ft) above 300 m, or 5 minutes per 600 m under some tables. For pressure canning, ADD PRESSURE instead: a weighted gauge goes from 10 psi to 15 psi above 300 m.
8. COOL undisturbed 12–24 h on a towel, no draught. Remove bands, test each seal by lifting the jar by the lid edge; a sealed lid is concave and does not flex. Label with contents and date. Store 10–21 °C, dark, bands OFF (a band can mask a failed seal).
DISCARD without tasting any jar that is unsealed, leaking, bulging, spurting on opening, mouldy, cloudy, foul-smelling, or has a lid that flexes. Suspect low-acid jars should be detoxified before disposal by boiling the contents 30 minutes, and the containers disinfected — botulinum toxin is destroyed by heat but the food must never be tasted to "check".

sections.heading: Drying: mathematics, methods and targets
sections.body:
Drying preserves by lowering water activity below the growth threshold of microbes. Moisture content on a wet basis is:
  MC% = (m_wet − m_dry) / m_wet × 100
where m_wet is the mass before drying and m_dry the bone-dry mass, both in grams. Targets: fruit 15–20% (leathery, no moisture when squeezed and torn), vegetables 5–10% (brittle, snaps), jerky ~15–20% (bends and cracks, does not snap), grain and beans 12–14% for safe long storage (above 14%, mould and insects thrive), herbs ~10% (crumbles).
A useful field rule for yield: mass lost ≈ starting mass × (MC_start − MC_end)/(100 − MC_end). Drying 1,000 g of apple at 84% moisture down to 18% removes 1,000 × (84−18)/(100−18) ≈ 805 g of water, leaving about 195 g.
METHODS:
• SUN DRYING needs ≥30 °C, low humidity (<60% RH), and moving air; racks 0.5 m off the ground, food in a single layer, netting against insects, brought in each night to avoid rehydration by dew. Best for grapes→raisins, tomatoes, chillies, apricots.
• SOLAR DRYER — a glazed collector box feeding a shaded drying chamber; reaches 55–70 °C and protects colour and vitamins.
• ELECTRIC DEHYDRATOR — fruit 57–60 °C for 6–16 h; vegetables 52–55 °C for 4–12 h; herbs 35–40 °C for 2–4 h (higher drives off volatile oils); jerky 63–68 °C.
• OVEN — lowest setting with the door propped 25–50 mm for vapour escape.
PRE-TREATMENT matters. BLANCH vegetables (steam 3–5 min or boil 2–3 min, then ice-water) to deactivate enzymes that would otherwise cause off-flavours and vitamin loss during storage. Dip light fruits in an ascorbic-acid solution (1 tsp powdered vitamin C or 1,500 mg crushed tablets per 500 mL water) or lemon juice 1:4 in water for 5 minutes to stop enzymatic browning. Cut uniformly — 3–6 mm slices dry evenly; thickness dominates drying time roughly as the square.
JERKY SAFETY: dehydrator temperatures alone do not reliably kill Salmonella and E. coli O157:H7 in raw meat. Either heat the strips to an internal 71 °C (160 °F) in marinade before drying, or dry first and then post-heat in a 135 °C oven for 10 minutes.
CONDITIONING: after drying, pack loosely in a sealed jar for 7–10 days, shaking daily. Residual moisture equalises between pieces; if condensation appears on the glass, return everything to the dryer. Then store in airtight, opaque containers with an oxygen absorber or desiccant; label and date. Shelf life at 15 °C: fruit 6–12 months, vegetables 6–12 months, properly dried grain in sealed containers with oxygen absorbers, many years.

sections.heading: Salting and brining
sections.body:
Salt (sodium chloride, NaCl) preserves by OSMOSIS: dissolved ions lower the water activity of the food's liquid phase and draw water out of microbial cells across their membranes, dehydrating and killing or arresting them. Roughly, aw falls about 0.005 for each 1% salt by weight in the water phase; a 10% brine phase gives aw ≈ 0.94, a 20% saturated brine aw ≈ 0.75.
MEASURING BRINE. Percentage brine by weight is:
  S% = mass of salt / (mass of salt + mass of water) × 100
Salometer/salinometer degrees express percentage of SATURATION, where 100° = fully saturated ≈ 26.4% salt by weight at 16 °C. So 10% salt by weight ≈ 38–40° salometer. Saturated brine floats a fresh egg high; a common field test is that an egg floats showing a coin-sized patch at about 10% salinity.
COMMON RATIOS:
• Vegetable fermentation (sauerkraut, kimchi): 2.0–2.5% salt by weight of vegetable — 20–25 g salt per kg of shredded cabbage. Enough to select for lactobacilli, not enough to stop them.
• Brined pickles (fermented cucumbers): 5–8% brine, held under the surface for 3–6 weeks.
• Fish salting (dry salt, klipfish/bacalao style): alternate layers of split fish and coarse salt at roughly 1 part salt to 3 parts fish by weight, pressed, drained daily, 3 weeks, then air-dried. Rehydrated by soaking 24–48 h with several water changes.
• Meat brine for flavour and moisture (not preservation): 5–6% salt, 1–12 h depending on thickness, refrigerated.
SALT TYPE MATTERS. Use pure non-iodised salt without anti-caking agents for fermentation and curing; iodine can inhibit some lactobacilli and anti-caking agents cloud the brine. Measure salt by WEIGHT, never volume — the same tablespoon holds about 18 g of fine table salt but only 10–12 g of flaky kosher salt, a nearly two-fold error.
Safety: salted foods must stay fully submerged beneath the brine (use a weight or a water-filled bag) — anything exposed to air grows mould and kahm yeast. Salt-preserved foods are extremely high in sodium; soaking and rinsing before use removes much of it. People on sodium-restricted diets should treat these as occasional foods and consult their clinician.

sections.heading: Curing and smoking — nitrite, safety and procedure
sections.body:
CURING means preserving meat with salt plus NITRITE (NO₂⁻) or NITRATE (NO₃⁻). Nitrite does three things nothing else does: it specifically inhibits Clostridium botulinum in the anaerobic interior of a sausage or ham; it reacts with myoglobin to form nitrosylmyoglobin, giving cured meat its stable pink colour; and it produces the characteristic cured flavour while retarding rancidity.
CURING SALTS (nomenclature varies by country; read the label and follow the manufacturer's ratio exactly):
• "Cure #1" / "pink salt" / Prague Powder #1 — 6.25% sodium nitrite in 93.75% salt, dyed pink so it is never mistaken for table salt. For cooked or short-cure products: bacon, ham, hot dogs, most smoked sausage. Standard use: 2.5 g per kg of meat (0.25%), delivering about 156 ppm nitrite — the common regulatory maximum.
• "Cure #2" — 6.25% sodium nitrite plus 4% sodium nitrate, for long dry-cured products (salami, coppa, prosciutto) where the nitrate acts as a slow reservoir converted to nitrite by bacteria over weeks or months.
TOXICITY WARNING: sodium nitrite is acutely poisonous. The estimated human lethal dose is in the region of 1 gram of pure nitrite; a few teaspoons of pink curing salt eaten directly can kill by methaemoglobinaemia. Store it labelled, sealed and away from children, and never scale a recipe by eye. Never substitute plain salt for cure or vice versa. Use a scale accurate to 0.1 g.
EQUILIBRIUM (EQ) CURING — the safest home method. Weigh the meat, then calculate every ingredient as a percentage of that mass: typically 2.0–2.75% salt, 0.25% Cure #1, 0–1% sugar, plus spices. Vacuum-seal or bag with all the cure, refrigerate at 2–4 °C, and hold roughly 1 day per 5 mm of thickness plus 2 days (a 50 mm pork belly ≈ 12 days), turning every couple of days. Because the total salt is fixed, the meat cannot become over-salted no matter how long it sits.
SMOKING is a preservation and flavour hurdle, not a substitute for curing:
• COLD SMOKE below 30 °C (86 °F) — flavours and dries but does NOT cook; the meat must already be cured, because these temperatures are squarely in the bacterial growth range.
• HOT SMOKE 60–90 °C — cooks and smokes together; take poultry to an internal 74 °C, whole cuts of pork and beef 63 °C with a 3-minute rest, minced/ground meat 71 °C, fish 63 °C, all measured at the thickest point with a calibrated probe.
Wood smoke deposits phenols and organic acids that are antimicrobial and antioxidant, but also polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons — heavily charred, heavily smoked meat is best eaten occasionally rather than daily. Use hardwoods (oak, hickory, apple, beech); never softwoods (pine, spruce — resinous, acrid), painted, treated, glued or salvaged timber.

sections.heading: Worked example and a preservation decision procedure
sections.body:
WORKED EXAMPLE — a 25 kg autumn cabbage harvest, no refrigeration, no pressure canner.
Cabbage is a LOW-ACID vegetable (pH ≈ 6.0), so plain canning in a boiling-water bath is unsafe and pressure canning is unavailable. Two safe routes remain: fermentation (which lowers pH below 4.6, after which water-bath canning also becomes an option) and drying.
Route chosen — sauerkraut. Trim and reserve 4 outer leaves. Net weight after trimming and coring: 22.0 kg. Salt at 2.25%: 22,000 g × 0.0225 = 495 g of non-iodised salt. Shred to 2–3 mm, layer with salt in a food-grade vessel, massage 10 minutes until brine runs freely, pack tightly to expel air, lay the reserved leaves on top, weight below the brine line, and cover with an airlock or loose cloth. Ferment 18–22 °C for 3–4 weeks (cooler = slower but better flavour; below 15 °C it may take 2 months). pH falls 6.0 → 4.5 within 2–3 days as Leuconostoc mesenteroides works, then to 3.4–3.6 as Lactobacillus plantarum takes over. Verify with pH strips or a meter before long storage. Then either keep cold (0–4 °C, keeps 6+ months) or hot-pack into jars and water-bath process 15 minutes for pints — now legitimate because the product is acid.
DECISION PROCEDURE for any food, in order:
1. Measure or look up the pH. Above 4.6 → the only shelf-stable options are pressure canning, drying to aw < 0.85, curing with nitrite, freezing, or acidification/fermentation to below 4.6.
2. Below 4.6 → water-bath canning, drying, sugar preserving, or fermentation all work.
3. Check what equipment and energy you actually have. Drying needs almost none; canning needs jars and heat; freezing needs uninterrupted power.
4. Stack at least two hurdles: salted AND dried, acid AND canned, cured AND cold-smoked AND chilled.
5. Label everything with contents and date, rotate oldest first, and inspect before eating.
COMMON MISTAKES: reusing flat canning lids; inventing or "lightening" recipes by cutting vinegar, salt or sugar; adding oil, flour, rice or dairy to canned goods (they slow heat penetration and are not covered by tested schedules); ignoring altitude; cooling jars in a draught (thermal shock cracks glass); storing with bands on; assuming a sealed lid alone proves safety. When any doubt exists — WHEN IN DOUBT, THROW IT OUT.

sections.heading: Pressure Canning: The Procedure for Low-Acid Foods, Step by Step
sections.body: Water-bath canning only reaches 100°C (212°F) at sea level — plenty to destroy yeasts, molds and most vegetative bacteria, but Clostridium botulinum spores shrug off boiling water for many hours. Low-acid foods (pH above 4.6 — most vegetables, meats, poultry, seafood) must instead be processed in a pressure canner, which traps steam under pressure to raise the internal temperature to 240°F (116°C) or higher, cutting the time needed for a lethal margin of safety down from many hours to tens of minutes.
steps: Wash jars, lids and rings in hot soapy water; keep jars hot in a low oven or in the canner itself so a cold jar doesn't crack when packed with hot food.

Prepare the low-acid food according to a tested recipe from a trusted current source (a university extension or USDA-style canning guide) — do not substitute jar sizes or ingredient ratios freely, since processing times are calculated for a specific density and headspace.

Pack jars, leaving the headspace the recipe specifies (commonly 1 inch/2.5 cm for most vegetables and meats) — too little headspace can prevent a proper seal, too much can leave food underprocessed at the top.

Wipe the jar rim clean of any food residue with a damp cloth, center a new lid, and screw the ring down to "fingertip tight" — tight enough to hold the lid, loose enough for trapped air to vent during processing.
Add the amount of water the canner manufacturer specifies to the canner base, load the jars onto the rack, and lock the lid.

Vent the canner: let steam escape steadily from the open petcock or weight for a full 10 minutes before pressurizing — this purges air pockets that would otherwise stop the canner reaching a true, even temperature at a given pressure reading.

Bring the canner up to the pressure your recipe specifies for your altitude (commonly 10 psi at sea level on a weighted-gauge canner, rising to 15 psi above roughly 1,000 ft/300 m; dial-gauge canners use different psi bands by altitude, so check your canner's own chart) and start timing only once that pressure is reached and holding steady.

Hold the pressure for the full processing time specified for that food and jar size (commonly 20–90 minutes depending on food density and jar size — pint jars of green beans run around 20 minutes, quart jars of meat can run 75–90 minutes), adjusting heat as needed to keep pressure steady rather than spiking, which risks liquid loss from the jars.

Turn off the heat and let the canner depressurize on its own — never force-cool it or remove the weight early, since a sudden pressure drop can boil the jars' contents violently out through the seal (siphoning) or make the gauge unreliable for the next batch.

Once the gauge reads zero, wait an additional 10 minutes, then unlock and open the lid away from your face, remove jars with a jar lifter, and set them undisturbed on a towel for 12–24 hours before checking that every lid has pulled down and sealed (a sealed lid does not flex when pressed in the center); refrigerate and use promptly any jar that fails to seal.

sections.heading: Freezing and Root-Cellaring: Preservation Without Removing Water
sections.body:
Canning, drying, salting and curing all preserve by pulling water out of reach of microbes — reducing water activity below the roughly 0.91 that most spoilage bacteria need. Freezing and cold storage take an entirely different route: they don't remove water at all, they simply slow the chemistry and biology down until it is negligible, which is why frozen food eventually spoils in weeks-to-years rather than being preserved indefinitely.

Water expands about 9% in volume when it freezes, and the rate of freezing determines how much damage that expansion does to a food's cell structure. A home freezer running at −18°C (0°F) cools slowly enough that ice crystals form large and jagged in the spaces between cells, rupturing cell walls as they grow — which is why thawed strawberries turn to mush while a commercial blast freezer at −40°C freezes the same fruit fast enough to form many tiny crystals that leave cell walls largely intact. This is also why refreezing a fully thawed food degrades texture further: it repeats the large-slow-crystal damage a second time.

Freezer burn is not spoilage in the microbial sense — it's sublimation, ice converting directly to vapor from a food's surface into the colder, drier air of the freezer, leaving a pale, dry, leathery patch. It is driven entirely by exposed surface area and imperfect sealing, which is why vacuum-sealed or tightly wrapped food resists it far longer than a loosely bagged item.

Vegetables destined for the freezer are usually blanched first — a brief plunge into boiling water (commonly 2–4 minutes depending on vegetable and piece size) followed immediately by an ice-water bath. This has nothing to do with killing microbes; its purpose is to destroy the vegetable's own enzymes (particularly peroxidase, whose persistence is the standard test for adequate blanching) that would otherwise slowly degrade color, flavor and texture for months even though the cold has stopped microbial growth.

Root cellaring works the opposite way from freezing: it holds food just above freezing, in a narrow temperature-and-humidity band mimicking winter soil. Most root vegetables keep best at 32–40°F (0–4°C) and 90–95% relative humidity. Potatoes are the exception: stored below about 40°F, their starch slowly converts to sugar, so they keep better nearer 45–50°F, and always away from light, which triggers greening and the buildup of the bitter, toxic alkaloid solanine just under the skin — any green-tinged potato flesh should be cut away generously or the potato discarded.

sections.heading: Getting the Gear
sections.body: Different preservation methods need different kit, but a well-stocked home canning-and-preserving shelf covers most of it; all of the following are widely sold at kitchen-supply, hardware or home-improvement stores.
ingredients: A water-bath canner (a tall lidded pot with a rack) for high-acid foods, and, separately, a pressure canner rated for canning (not a generic stovetop pressure cooker) with a working dial or weighted gauge for low-acid foods.
Wide-mouth and regular-mouth glass canning jars in pint and quart sizes, with new two-piece lids each canning season (the flat lid's sealing compound is single-use) and reusable screw rings.
A jar lifter, a magnetic lid wand, a canning funnel and a plastic (non-metal) headspace/bubble tool — inexpensive canning-utensil sets bundle all four.
A digital probe thermometer and an accurate dial or weighted-gauge pressure canner gauge (some extension offices will test a dial gauge's accuracy for free or low cost).
A food dehydrator with an adjustable thermostat and a fan (or a well-ventilated oven set to its lowest temperature with the door propped) plus mesh drying trays or racks.
A digital kitchen scale, for weighing salt-to-food ratios precisely in brining and curing.

Curing (pink) salt — a sodium nitrite blend sold at butcher-supply or well-stocked kitchen stores, kept away from plain table salt and clearly labeled, since it is toxic in bulk and is formulated to be used only in small, measured curing doses.
A hygrometer/thermometer combo for smokehouses or curing chambers, and food-grade curing chamber space (even a spare refrigerator with a humidity controller) for dry-cured items.
Oxygen absorbers and moisture-proof storage containers (food-grade buckets with gasketed lids, or heavy foil pouches) for finished dried goods.

sections.heading: Recognizing Spoilage and Canning Failures Before They Reach the Table
sections.body:
Every preservation method above can fail, and knowing the warning signs is as important as knowing the procedure, because the most dangerous failures — particularly botulism — often produce no smell, taste or visible spoilage at all.

A canning jar that has failed to seal properly is the most common and most visible failure: press the center of a cooled lid — a properly sealed lid stays concave and does not flex or click. An unsealed jar should be refrigerated and used within days, or reprocessed with a fresh lid within 24 hours; never simply store it on the shelf and hope. A lid that seals but later pops up, or a jar that spurts liquid when opened, or contents that look cloudy, foamy, or show gas bubbles, are all signs of active microbial growth after the fact — discard the entire contents without tasting, pour it out where no person or animal will contact it, and boil any surface it may have splashed onto for 10 minutes, since botulinum toxin itself (unlike the spore) is inactivated by boiling but can be present without any of these visible cues in a small fraction of failures.

"Flat sour" spoilage is a subtler failure specific to canned vegetables: the jar seals normally and shows no gas or cloudiness, but a heat-tolerant acid-producing bacterium has survived processing and soured the contents — the only tell is an off, sour smell or taste on opening, which is why any canned low-acid food that smells or tastes even slightly "off" should be discarded rather than tasted further to confirm.

Dried foods fail differently: mold is the main risk, usually from inadequate drying or from being packaged before fully cooled, letting condensation form inside the container. Any moldy dried food should be discarded entirely rather than having the moldy portion cut away, since mold's hyphae and any mycotoxins it produces typically extend well beyond the visible spot.

Cured and smoked meats show failure as sliminess, a grey-green discoloration distinct from the pink curing color, or a sharp ammonia-like smell — all signs the curing salt concentration, time, or temperature control fell short during the slow process, and none of these products should ever be tasted to check.

guides.title: The Science of Fermentation — Bread, Alcohol, Yogurt & Kraut
guides.summary: How microbes convert sugar into acid, alcohol and gas: the biochemistry of glycolysis and its branches, the organisms responsible, and complete working procedures with weights, temperatures, times and pH targets for sourdough bread, beer and wine, yogurt and cheese, and vegetable ferments.

sections.heading: What fermentation is, chemically
sections.body:
FERMENTATION is the anaerobic (oxygen-free) extraction of energy from an organic substrate, in which an organic molecule — not oxygen — serves as the final electron acceptor. Every fermentation begins with GLYCOLYSIS (the Embden–Meyerhof–Parnas pathway), which splits one glucose into two pyruvate molecules:
  C₆H₁₂O₆ + 2 NAD⁺ + 2 ADP + 2 Pᵢ → 2 CH₃COCOO⁻ + 2 NADH + 2 ATP + 2 H⁺
Here NAD⁺/NADH is the cell's electron carrier, ADP + Pᵢ → ATP is the energy currency, and Pᵢ is inorganic phosphate. Glycolysis stalls unless NADH is re-oxidised back to NAD⁺. With oxygen present, respiration does this and yields ~30–32 ATP per glucose. Without oxygen, the cell dumps the electrons onto pyruvate or its derivatives — that dumping IS fermentation, and it yields only 2 ATP per glucose.
THE THREE BRANCHES THAT MATTER IN FOOD:
• ALCOHOLIC (yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae): pyruvate → acetaldehyde + CO₂, then acetaldehyde + NADH → ethanol. Net: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂. By mass, 100 g glucose theoretically yields 51.1 g ethanol and 48.9 g CO₂; real yields are 90–95% of that because yeast diverts some carbon to its own growth and to glycerol.
• HOMOLACTIC (Lactobacillus, Streptococcus): pyruvate + NADH → lactate. Net: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 CH₃CH(OH)COOH. One product, essentially no gas — this is yogurt.
• HETEROLACTIC (Leuconostoc, Lactobacillus brevis, via the phosphoketolase pathway): C₆H₁₂O₆ → lactate + ethanol + CO₂. Gas, acid and aroma together — this is early-stage sauerkraut, kefir and sourdough's complexity.
A fourth, ACETIC fermentation (Acetobacter), is technically an aerobic oxidation, not a true fermentation: C₂H₅OH + O₂ → CH₃COOH + H₂O. It makes vinegar and spoils wine.
Preservation follows from the chemistry: lactic and acetic acids drop the pH below the tolerance of pathogens, ethanol above ~12% is itself antimicrobial, CO₂ displaces oxygen, and the fermenting organisms outcompete spoilers for nutrients while secreting bacteriocins (protein antibiotics such as nisin).

sections.heading: Vegetable ferments — sauerkraut, kimchi, pickles
sections.body:
Lacto-fermentation of vegetables is a spontaneous SUCCESSION of naturally present bacteria, selected by salt and anaerobiosis. Nothing is added but salt.
THE SUCCESSION:
1. Days 0–2 — aerobic and coliform bacteria bloom, then die back as oxygen is consumed and acid appears.
2. Days 2–5 — Leuconostoc mesenteroides (heterolactic, salt- and cold-tolerant) drives pH from ~6.0 down to ~4.5, producing CO₂ (visible bubbling), lactate, acetate, ethanol and the aromatic esters that give kraut its character. It self-limits near pH 4.0.
3. Days 5–21 — Lactobacillus plantarum and L. brevis (homolactic, acid-tolerant) take over and finish at pH 3.4–3.6, total acidity 1.5–2.0% as lactic acid.
MASTER PROCEDURE (sauerkraut):
• Shred cabbage to 2–3 mm. Weigh it — this is the only measurement that matters.
• Add non-iodised salt at 2.0–2.5% of that weight (20–25 g per kg). Below 1.5% the ferment goes soft and risks spoilage; above 3% the lactobacilli are inhibited and the result is merely salty.
• Massage or pound 5–10 minutes until the cabbage releases enough brine to cover itself. Pack into a jar or crock, pressing out all air pockets.
• Submerge everything below the brine with a weight — a water-filled bag, a glass disc, or a folded outer leaf under a stone. EXPOSED VEGETABLE = MOULD.
• Vent CO₂: an airlock, or unscrew the lid daily ("burp") to avoid a burst jar.
• Hold 18–22 °C for 2–4 weeks. Taste weekly. When sour enough, refrigerate; cold storage nearly halts the ferment and it keeps 6+ months.
BRINE (rather than dry-salt) method, for cucumbers, carrots, beans, whole vegetables: 3–5% brine — 30–50 g salt dissolved per litre of unchlorinated water — poured to cover, everything weighted down, 1–4 weeks.
KIMCHI adds a stage: brine napa cabbage in 5–8% salt 2–4 h (or dry-salt 1–2 h), rinse, drain, then coat with a paste of gochugaru chilli flakes, garlic, ginger, spring onion and often a starch porridge and fish sauce; ferment 1–3 days at room temperature, then refrigerate for weeks of slow development.
TROUBLESHOOTING: a white, flat, wrinkly film is KAHM YEAST — harmless, skim it off, but it signals oxygen exposure or too little salt. Fuzzy blue, green, black or pink growth is MOULD — for a fully submerged brine ferment many traditions skim and continue, but the cautious and correct advice is to discard the batch, since mould hyphae penetrate below the surface and some species make mycotoxins. Slimy or ropy brine means the ferment was too warm or too low in salt. Soft kraut means too little salt or too much heat. A rotten, putrid smell (as opposed to sharp and sour) means discard.

sections.heading: Dairy ferments — yogurt, kefir and simple cheese
sections.body:
Milk contains ~4.8% lactose (glucose+galactose), ~3.3% protein (80% casein, 20% whey), ~3.5% fat. Lactic acid bacteria convert lactose to lactic acid; as pH falls, the negatively charged casein micelles lose their repulsive surface charge and at their ISOELECTRIC POINT of pH 4.6 they aggregate into a gel — that gel is yogurt, and pressed and drained it is fresh cheese.
YOGURT PROCEDURE:
1. HEAT 1 L milk to 82–85 °C and hold 20–30 minutes (or 90 °C for 5–10 min). This is not sterilisation — it denatures β-lactoglobulin, the main whey protein, so it binds to casein and makes a firmer, less weepy gel. Skipping this step is the single commonest cause of thin yogurt.
2. COOL to 43 °C (110 °F). Above 46 °C the culture is damaged; below 38 °C it sets slowly and sourly.
3. INOCULATE with 2–3% starter: 20–30 mL of live plain yogurt per litre, or a commercial freeze-dried culture. The classic pair is Streptococcus thermophilus and Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus, which grow PROTOCOOPERATIVELY: S. thermophilus consumes oxygen and releases formic acid and CO₂ that stimulate L. bulgaricus, which in turn releases amino acids and peptides that feed S. thermophilus. Together they ferment about twice as fast as either alone.
4. INCUBATE undisturbed at 42–45 °C for 4–8 hours until pH ≈ 4.5 and the gel does not flow when the pot is tilted. Then chill promptly; cold arrests acidification. Greek-style yogurt is simply yogurt drained in cloth for 2–6 h, removing whey and roughly doubling protein per spoon.
KEFIR is different: a symbiotic community of ~30–50 species of bacteria and yeasts held in a polysaccharide (kefiran) matrix — the "grains". Add 1–2 tablespoons of grains per 500 mL milk, ferment 18–25 °C for 12–24 h, strain, reuse the grains indefinitely. Because yeasts are involved it is mildly effervescent and contains 0.2–2% ethanol.
SIMPLE ACID CHEESE (paneer/queso fresco): heat 2 L whole milk to 85 °C, remove from heat, stir in 60 mL lemon juice or vinegar a little at a time until the curd separates cleanly from greenish whey (about 1 minute), rest 10 minutes, ladle into cloth, drain 30 minutes, press under a 2 kg weight for 1–2 h. Yield roughly 300–400 g. RENNET cheeses instead use chymosin, an enzyme that cleaves the κ-casein hair layer at a specific bond, letting micelles fuse at near-neutral pH — this gives an elastic curd that can be aged, unlike the crumbly acid curd.
SAFETY: use pasteurised milk unless you know your raw-milk source and accept the documented risk of Listeria, Salmonella, Campylobacter and E. coli O157:H7 — these are particularly dangerous in pregnancy, childhood, old age and immunosuppression. Cultured products are not a treatment for any disease; discuss probiotics with a clinician if you are immunocompromised.

sections.heading: Sourdough — the leavening symbiosis
sections.body:
A SOURDOUGH STARTER is a stable co-culture of wild yeasts (commonly Kazachstania humilis or Saccharomyces cerevisiae) and lactic acid bacteria (Fructilactobacillus sanfranciscensis and relatives), typically at a bacteria:yeast ratio near 100:1. The yeasts make CO₂ (leavening) and ethanol; the bacteria make lactic and acetic acid (flavour, preservation, gluten conditioning). The partnership is stable because the dominant yeast cannot metabolise maltose, which the bacteria prefer to leave alone, while the bacteria tolerate the acidity that excludes competitors.
CREATING A STARTER (7–14 days):
• Day 1: mix 50 g wholemeal flour + 50 g water at ~28 °C in a jar, cover loosely.
• Days 2–4: it may bubble early from Leuconostoc and coliforms and then go quiet and smell odd — this is normal succession, not failure. Once daily, discard all but 50 g and feed 50 g flour + 50 g water.
• Days 5–14: feed twice daily. It is ready when it reliably doubles or triples in 4–8 hours after feeding and smells cleanly yogurty-tangy. pH stabilises at 3.5–4.3.
• Maintenance: at 20–24 °C feed daily at 1:1:1 (starter:flour:water by weight); refrigerated, feed weekly.
BAKER'S PERCENTAGE is the trade's arithmetic: every ingredient is expressed as a percentage of TOTAL FLOUR weight, which is always 100%. A 75% hydration loaf with 1,000 g flour has 750 g water. HYDRATION = water ÷ flour × 100.
BASIC COUNTRY LOAF (makes one ~900 g loaf):
1. Levain: 20 g starter + 100 g flour + 100 g water; 4–8 h at 24 °C until domed and bubbly.
2. Autolyse: mix 800 g bread flour + 200 g wholemeal + 720 g water (72% hydration), rest 45 minutes. During autolyse, flour proteases and the simple hydration of glutenin and gliadin begin building the gluten network with no kneading.
3. Add all the levain and 20 g salt (2% of flour); mix thoroughly.
4. BULK FERMENT 4–5 h at 24–26 °C, folding the dough over itself 4 times at 30–45 minute intervals for the first 2 hours. Bulk is done when the dough has risen 30–50%, is domed and jiggly, and shows bubbles at the edges.
5. Pre-shape, rest 20–30 min, final shape with tension, place seam-up in a floured basket.
6. PROOF 1–2 h at room temperature, or 8–16 h at 4 °C (cold retard develops acetic acid and sour flavour and makes scoring easier).
7. BAKE in a preheated covered Dutch oven at 250 °C for 20 minutes (trapped steam keeps the crust elastic for maximum oven spring), then uncovered at 230 °C for 20–25 minutes to an internal temperature of 96–99 °C.
WHAT THE HEAT DOES: yeast activity peaks then dies near 60 °C; starch GELATINISES from 60–85 °C, absorbing water and setting the crumb; gluten proteins coagulate ~74 °C; the crust browns by Maillard and caramelisation above 150 °C. Sourdough's acidity also degrades phytate, improving mineral availability, and slows starch retrogradation so the loaf stales more slowly.
COMMON MISTAKES: using a starter that is not at peak activity; under-fermenting (dense, gummy crumb) or over-fermenting (slack dough, flat loaf, sour and pasty); adding salt before hydration is complete; opening the oven early; slicing hot bread before the starch has set.

sections.heading: Alcoholic fermentation — beer, wine, cider
sections.body:
Yeast needs FERMENTABLE SUGAR. Fruit supplies it directly; grain supplies starch that must first be converted, which is what malting and mashing do.
MEASURING SUGAR AND ALCOHOL. Specific gravity (SG) is the density of the liquid divided by that of water (1.000). Sugar raises it. Alcohol by volume is estimated as:
  ABV% ≈ (OG − FG) × 131.25
where OG is original gravity before fermentation and FG is final gravity after. Example: OG 1.055, FG 1.010 → (0.045) × 131.25 ≈ 5.9% ABV. Degrees Brix (°Bx) express grams of sucrose per 100 g solution; °Bx ≈ (SG − 1) × 1000 / 4.
WINE / CIDER (simplest route):
1. Crush fruit or press juice. Target OG 1.080–1.095 for wine (≈11–13% ABV), 1.045–1.060 for cider. Add sugar if needed: roughly 17 g of sugar per litre raises SG by 0.007 and gives ~1% ABV.
2. Optionally add potassium metabisulphite at ~50 ppm SO₂ (about ¼ Campden tablet per 4.5 L) and wait 24 hours; this stuns wild organisms so your chosen yeast dominates. Skip it for a spontaneous ferment and accept more variability.
3. Pitch a wine yeast (e.g. Saccharomyces cerevisiae EC-1118 or 71B) at ~1 g per 4–5 L, plus yeast nutrient if the juice is low in nitrogen.
4. PRIMARY ferment 18–24 °C for 5–10 days under a loose cover, then rack (siphon off the sediment) into a vessel with an AIRLOCK — a one-way water seal that lets CO₂ out and keeps oxygen and vinegar bacteria out.
5. SECONDARY 2–8 weeks until the airlock is silent and gravity is stable across three days (FG typically 0.990–1.000 dry).
6. Rack again, age, and bottle. To carbonate, add priming sugar at 6–8 g per litre and bottle in pressure-rated bottles — plain wine bottles or jars can explode.
BEER adds a mash: malted barley (grain germinated then kiln-dried, which develops α- and β-amylase) is milled and steeped in water at 63–70 °C for 60 minutes. β-amylase (optimum ~63 °C) makes maltose and a thinner, drier beer; α-amylase (optimum ~70 °C) leaves more unfermentable dextrins and a fuller body. The sweet wort is then boiled 60 minutes with hops (isomerising alpha acids into bitter iso-alpha acids and sterilising the wort), cooled rapidly to 18–20 °C for ale yeast or 10–12 °C for lager yeast, and fermented 1–2 weeks.
SANITATION is the whole game. Everything touching the cooled wort or juice must be sanitised — an unrinsed no-rinse acid sanitiser, or 1 tablespoon unscented household bleach per 4.5 L water with 10 minutes of contact and a thorough rinse. Clean first, sanitise second; sanitiser does not work through dirt.
SAFETY AND LEGALITY: home brewing and winemaking are legal in many jurisdictions within volume limits, but DISTILLATION is a licensed activity almost everywhere and is dangerous — never distil without legal authorisation. Never ferment in sealed rigid containers (explosion). Never use galvanised, copper-corroded, lead-glazed or non-food-grade plastic vessels. Fermenting vessels release large volumes of CO₂: ferment in a ventilated space, because CO₂ is heavier than air and can pool at floor level in a cellar to asphyxiating concentrations.

sections.heading: Controlling a ferment: the five variables
sections.body:
Every fermentation is steered by the same five levers. Adjust these and you can direct almost any process.
1. TEMPERATURE — the master control. Roughly, microbial rates double for each 10 °C rise (a Q₁₀ of 2) until enzymes denature. Yogurt 42–45 °C, kefir 20–25 °C, sauerkraut 18–22 °C, ale yeast 18–22 °C, lager yeast 10–12 °C, sourdough 24–28 °C. Cool ferments run slower but produce more aromatic complexity and fewer harsh fusel alcohols; hot ferments are fast, blunt and prone to off-flavours.
2. SALT — selects for halotolerant lactobacilli and slows everything. 2.0–2.5% for kraut, 3–5% brine for pickles, 5–8% for long fish or olive cures. Every 1% of salt roughly doubles the fermentation time.
3. OXYGEN — most food ferments want none after the start. Submerge solids, use airlocks, minimise headspace. Exceptions: vinegar (needs air), koji and tempeh (moulds are aerobic and need airflow).
4. pH AND ACIDITY — the safety metric. Verify with pH strips (±0.2 accuracy is adequate) or a calibrated meter. Targets: sauerkraut and kimchi 3.4–4.0; yogurt 4.2–4.6; sourdough 3.5–4.3; a finished pickle below 4.6 for shelf stability. A ferment that has not dropped below pH 4.6 within 48 hours at room temperature has failed — discard it.
5. INOCULUM — spontaneous (relying on the microbes already present on the vegetable or fruit) or with a defined starter. Backslopping — adding 2–5% of a previous successful batch — is the traditional middle path: it accelerates acidification, crowding out spoilers during the vulnerable first 24 hours.
A WORKED CONTROL EXAMPLE: a kraut fermenting at 28 °C in a warm kitchen went soft and slightly off within 5 days. Diagnosis: temperature too high (favours pectinolytic and spoilage organisms over L. plantarum) and salt likely under 1.5%. Correction for the next batch: weigh the cabbage precisely, salt at 2.5% (25 g/kg), move to a 17–19 °C cellar, and backslop 3% brine from a good previous batch to drop pH below 4.5 within 48 hours. Result: firm, clean kraut at pH 3.5 in 3 weeks.

sections.heading: Nutrition, benefits and hard safety limits
sections.body:
WHAT FERMENTATION DOES FOR NUTRITION:
• Predigests macronutrients — proteases release free amino acids and peptides, so fermented foods are often easier to digest. Yogurt and aged cheese contain far less lactose than milk, which is why many lactose-intolerant people tolerate them.
• Degrades ANTINUTRIENTS — phytic acid (which chelates iron, zinc, calcium and magnesium) is broken down by microbial and cereal phytases during sourdough fermentation and legume soaking/fermentation, measurably improving mineral absorption. Tempeh fermentation reduces oligosaccharides that cause flatulence.
• Synthesises vitamins — lactic acid bacteria and yeasts produce folate, riboflavin and, in some bacterial ferments (natto, tempeh with certain bacteria), vitamin B12. Do NOT rely on plant ferments for B12: content is erratic and often consists of inactive analogues. Use a validated supplement or fortified food.
• Removes toxins — the classic case is cassava, whose cyanogenic glycosides (linamarin) are largely eliminated by grating and fermenting for 3–5 days before cooking. Undetoxified bitter cassava causes acute cyanide poisoning and the paralytic disease konzo.
• Supplies live microbes — many fermented foods deliver 10⁶–10⁹ colony-forming units per gram. Evidence supports modest benefits for some digestive complaints; claims of curing disease are not supported.
HARD SAFETY LIMITS:
• Never ferment low-acid foods in an oil medium or seal them anaerobically without acidification — garlic-in-oil and improperly handled fermented fish/marine mammal products are documented botulism vehicles. Garlic in oil must be refrigerated and used within days, or acidified.
• Never ferment meat without proper cure (nitrite) and a validated protocol; charcuterie is the one ferment where amateur improvisation kills.
• Verify pH for anything you intend to store outside a refrigerator.
• Discard on any sign of fuzzy mould, pink/orange/black growth, sliminess, gas in a product that should not gas, or a putrid rather than sour smell. A sour, sharp, yeasty or cheesy smell is right; rotten, faecal or solvent-like is not.
• People who are pregnant, immunocompromised, very young or very old should be conservative with raw-milk products and homemade ferments generally.
This is educational material. Fermented foods interact with medication (aged, tyramine-rich cheeses and MAO inhibitors; alcohol with many drugs) and with conditions such as histamine intolerance. Consult a qualified clinician for personal medical guidance.

sections.heading: Microbial Succession: Who Wins Inside a Jar, and When
sections.body:
A jar of fresh-cut cabbage in 2% brine does not become sauerkraut through the action of one organism — it runs through an entire ecological succession over a few weeks, and classic mid-20th-century food-science studies (most famously the sauerkraut fermentation work by Carl Pederson) mapped out a pattern that holds for most vegetable ferments.

At the start, the vegetable's natural surface flora is a mixed bag: various coliform-type Enterobacteriaceae, some aerobic spoilage bacteria, wild yeasts, and only a small population of lactic acid bacteria (LAB). Salt and the exclusion of air narrow the field first — 2–3% salt draws water out of plant cells by osmosis (creating the brine) while inhibiting many spoilage organisms more than it inhibits salt-tolerant LAB, and the anaerobic environment inside a submerged, weighted ferment shuts down the aerobic spoilers almost immediately.

Into that narrowed field, Leuconostoc mesenteroides is usually first to bloom — a heterofermentative LAB producing not just lactic acid but also CO2, ethanol and mannitol. The CO2 physically displaces remaining oxygen (visible as bubbling in the first few days) while the acid drops pH from a starting ~6.5 toward 4.5. But Leuconostoc is relatively acid-sensitive, and as pH keeps falling it is progressively out-competed by the more acid-tolerant Lactobacillus plantarum, a homofermentative LAB that converts sugar almost entirely to lactic acid, driving pH down further, often to around 3.5. It is this final, most acid-tolerant population that both preserves the ferment long-term and gives finished sauerkraut its cleaner, sharper sourness compared to the more complex, faintly effervescent flavor of the earlier Leuconostoc-dominated stage — and why traditional recipes that skim early foam rather than panic at it are right to do so, since that foam is normal CO2 and yeast activity, not a sign of failure, so long as the brine stays cloudy-but-not-slimy and smells sharply sour rather than putrid.

sections.heading: Vinegar and the Second Fermentation: Turning Alcohol Into Acid
sections.body:
Every alcoholic ferment described elsewhere in this guide can, left open to the air, run a second fermentation that converts it into vinegar. Where yeast fermentation and lactic-acid fermentation are both fundamentally anaerobic processes, vinegar-making flips that requirement — it is strictly aerobic, and depends on a different group of organisms: acetic acid bacteria, most commonly Acetobacter species.

Acetobacter oxidizes ethanol to acetaldehyde and then to acetic acid using membrane-bound enzymes that sit on the cell's outer surface specifically so they can access dissolved atmospheric oxygen directly — net reaction CH3CH2OH + O2 → CH3COOH + H2O. This is why a wine or hard cider left uncorked and exposed to air will, given weeks and warmth (roughly 25–30°C is ideal for Acetobacter), turn to vinegar whether you want it to or not, and why sealed, anaerobic storage is the actual defense against "the wine going off," not any special vinegar-specific spoilage.

A visible byproduct is the "mother of vinegar" — a rubbery, translucent mat that forms at the liquid's surface, made of cellulose the Acetobacter bacteria secrete to hold their colony at the air-liquid interface where oxygen is most available. It is harmless, edible, and is in fact the traditional starter culture used to seed a new batch, functioning the same way a sourdough starter or a kombucha SCOBY does for their respective ferments. Commercial vinegar production simply industrializes this same reaction, either slowly (essentially a managed open barrel) or quickly by trickling alcohol over a large surface area of wood shavings packed with acetic bacteria to maximize oxygen contact, cutting the process from months to under a day.

sections.heading: Mould-Based Ferments: Koji, Miso, Tempeh and the Enzyme Route
sections.body:
Every ferment covered so far in this guide is bacterial or yeast-driven; a fourth major branch uses filamentous moulds instead, and it underpins an entire cuisine's worth of staple foods: koji-based ferments and tempeh.

Koji is rice, barley or soybeans inoculated with spores of Aspergillus oryzae, a mould selectively bred over centuries for one specific talent: it secretes enormous quantities of amylase and protease enzymes directly into the grain it's growing on. Amylase hydrolyzes starch into simple sugars, and protease hydrolyzes protein into free amino acids and peptides — meaning koji doesn't ferment the food itself so much as pre-digest it chemically, producing a sweet, savory, glutamate-rich substrate a second organism can then actually ferment. This is the hidden first stage behind sake (koji's sugars feed a subsequent yeast fermentation into alcohol, all in the same vessel — an unusual "multiple parallel fermentation" not seen in wine or beer), soy sauce and miso (where the sugars and amino acids are then fermented further by salt-tolerant yeasts and LAB over months, developing deep umami from free glutamate), and rice vinegar.

Tempeh works on a different mould principle entirely. Cooked, dehulled soybeans are inoculated with Rhizopus oligosporus, whose mycelium grows as a dense white mat of thread-like hyphae that physically binds the individual beans into a firm, sliceable cake. The mould still contributes some enzymatic breakdown of the beans' proteins and fats, but its most visible contribution is purely structural, and tempeh is eaten with the living mycelium mat intact rather than filtered or aged away. Because Rhizopus needs oxygen to grow — unlike the strict LAB anaerobes elsewhere in this guide — tempeh is fermented in shallow, perforated or lightly vented containers rather than sealed jars: too little airflow and the mould won't establish; too much and the beans dry out before the mycelium can bind them.

sections.heading: Getting the Gear
sections.body: A surprising amount of fermentation needs no special equipment beyond clean jars, but a few purpose-made tools make the difference between guessing and actually controlling a ferment, and all of them are sold at home-brewing or kitchen-supply stores.
ingredients: Wide-mouth glass fermentation jars or a ceramic fermentation crock with a water-sealed lid, for vegetable ferments.
Fermentation weights (glass or ceramic discs) to keep vegetables submerged under their brine, since anything poking above the liquid surface is exposed to air and can mold.
A digital kitchen scale accurate to 1 g, essential for weighing salt as a percentage of vegetable weight rather than guessing by volume.
pH test strips (a cheap, wide-range set) or, for more precision, a digital pH meter with calibration solution, to confirm a ferment has dropped below a safe threshold.
An airlock (a small one-way valve, sold at any home-brew supply store) fitted through a drilled stopper or lid, for alcoholic ferments and sealed sourdough starters.
A hydrometer and a tall glass or plastic test jar, for measuring sugar content before and alcohol content after an alcoholic ferment.

A live starter culture appropriate to the ferment — dairy kefir grains, a kombucha SCOBY, active sourdough starter, wine or beer yeast, or koji spores — sold at home-brew shops, specialty grocers, or by mail from small-batch culture suppliers; a spoonful from an existing healthy culture also works to inoculate a new batch.
A dairy or candy thermometer, for holding yogurt and cheese cultures within their narrow active temperature range.
Non-iodized, non-anticaking salt (plain pickling or canning salt) — iodine and anticaking agents can inhibit fermentation or cloud the brine.
Clean cloth or coffee filters and rubber bands, to cover open ferments so airborne wild yeast can reach them while dust and insects can't.

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Running and Measuring Your Own Controlled Ferment
sections.body: Sauerkraut is the simplest possible ferment to instrument, because its variables map directly onto the five-variable framework described elsewhere in this guide, and the whole thing can be tracked with a scale and pH strips.
steps: Weigh a head of cabbage after shredding it (discard the tough core); note the exact weight in grams — say 1,000 g for a worked example.
Calculate salt at 2% of that weight (1,000 g × 0.02 = 20 g) and weigh it out precisely rather than measuring by volume, since salt density varies by brand and crystal size.
Massage the salt into the shredded cabbage by hand for 5–10 minutes until it releases enough liquid to pool visibly in the bowl — this is the brine, drawn out by osmosis.
Pack the cabbage and its released liquid tightly into a clean jar, pressing down firmly to eliminate air pockets, leaving about 2 inches (5 cm) of headspace.

Place a fermentation weight on top to hold all solids fully submerged under the brine; top up with a 2% salt-brine solution (20 g salt per 1,000 mL water) if the cabbage's own liquid doesn't fully cover it.
Cover loosely (a cloth and rubber band, or a lid set on but not sealed tight) and set the jar out of direct sunlight at room temperature, ideally 18–22°C (65–72°F).

Check daily for the first week: press any solids back under the brine if they float up, and expect visible bubbling and cloudiness in the first 2–5 days — this is the normal Leuconostoc-dominated early stage, not a fault.

Starting on day 3, dip a clean pH strip into the brine every 2–3 days and log the reading against the date; watch pH fall from a starting point near 6.0–6.5 toward the 3.5–4.0 range as Lactobacillus plantarum takes over.

Taste-test with a clean utensil once pH reads below about 4.0 (commonly 1–4 weeks depending on room temperature); when the flavor and sourness suit you, move the jar to the refrigerator, which slows the ferment nearly to a stop.

Discard the entire batch without tasting further if at any point you see fuzzy mold (as opposed to harmless white kahm yeast film, which can simply be skimmed off) or if it smells rotten rather than sharply sour — log the outcome either way, since a personal record of salt %, temperature and days-to-target-pH across a few batches is what actually lets you control future ferments rather than guess.

guides.title: Cooking Chemistry — Heat, the Maillard Reaction & Emulsions
